alternatives.root_cause: A runtime flag flip in flagd turned on a failing code path inside fraud-detection, explaining errors with no change records.
alternatives.why_not: The empty change logs fit, but there is no application-level exception on a flagged path in the log; the visible failures are connectivity/host-resolution failures, and flagd itself answered other callers normally.

alternatives.root_cause: flagd became slow, so fraud-detection failed waiting on flag evaluation.
alternatives.why_not: flagd's error ratio is unchanged from baseline and its spans for cart and load-generator complete in well under 10 ms in the incident window.

alternatives.root_cause: fraud-detection's process was stopped while its socket still accepted, hanging callers.
alternatives.why_not: A frozen process writes nothing; fraud-detection emitted errors and stack traces during the incident window.

verdict.summary: fraud-detection lost network connectivity (DNS/egress) to its dependencies around 16:51, so its outbound calls — telemetry export to the collector and its long-lived flagd evaluation stream — failed or hung to timeout while fraud-detection itself kept running and logging the failures.
verdict.reasoning: fraud-detection is the only service whose error ratio departed from baseline (tr_f3ebd780c326), with long stretches of no traffic at all rather than a steady error rate. Its own log around onset is dominated by host-resolution failures on an outbound dependency and stack traces, i.e. the process is alive and complaining it cannot reach things (tr_1d387c8dd1e1, tr_0a0a168e6f08) — that excludes process_freeze, which would be silent. The suspected downstream, flagd, is demonstrably healthy: its error ratio is flat versus baseline (tr_7d7ecfad0a59) and it serves cart and load-generator evaluations in single-digit milliseconds in the same window (tr_a9265f107142), so flagd is not slow or broken; the only pathological flagd interaction is fraud-detection's own long-lived evaluation stream that ended in a server-side timeout (tr_e1e52988628b), exactly what a caller cut off from the network looks like. Change logs for both fraud-detection and flagd are empty over 24 h (tr_3752aed0b9e1, tr_92f097feae75), so no artifact or config edit is in play. flagd's own log window held nothing (tr_a181df7a468e), consistent with it simply not being the failing party rather than with it being frozen, given its healthy traces.
open_questions: Whether the connectivity loss is DNS-specific or full egress isolation — only one unresolvable hostname is visible in the kept log lines.
Whether fraud-detection's Kafka consumption stopped at the same moment as the flagd/collector failures; the elided middle of the log window hides when record consumption ceased.
Whether the long flagd stream timeout began before onset (it started ~16:11) and is therefore a separate, pre-existing condition rather than part of this partition.
